items.title: In Defense of the Unsharp Photo
items.summary: Take a look at the three unedited photos below. Technically speaking, none of these shots are "perfect." They aren't sharp, at least not in that hyper-crisp, digital way that dominates social media and magazines today. There's a simple reason for it. I shot them on…
items.content_html:
Take a look at the three unedited photos below.
 
 
 
 

Technically speaking, none of these shots are "perfect." They aren't sharp, at least not in that hyper-crisp, digital way that dominates social media and magazines today.

There's a simple reason for it. I shot them on vintage film cameras loaded with ISO 100 film, which meant slower shutter speeds and a shallower depth of field. Layer on top the characteristics of older glass, lenses that simply lack the clinical, razor-sharp edge of modern optics, and the result is softer by nature.

Why I love the soft look

To me, that lack of clinical sharpness is precisely where the soul, energy, and character of an image live. There is an organic warmth to the frames that makes me immediately want to see them printed the traditional way in a darkroom.

Henri Cartier-Bresson famously called sharpness a "bourgeois concept," and long before I ever stumbled across his quote, that mindset had already been shaping how I approach my work.

Knowing when sharpness actually matters

Of course, technical perfection has its place. When you're on a commercial job, shooting products, or capturing architectural interiors, the final images need to be pin-sharp. No question about it.

But photography isn't just about chasing resolution, tweaking color profiles, or relying on camera specs to manufacture a vibe. It’s a visual language meant to communicate emotion, feeling, and mood. More often than not, I find far more feeling in photos that are technically not correct. What good is a technically flawless photo if it leaves you completely cold?

As Daido Moriyama pointed out, you can write a breathtaking poem with a cheap ballpoint pen. The tool in your hand is secondary to the story you want to tell.

The power of leaving room to feel

There is a quiet power in simplicity and understatement, leaving room for interpretation lets the core message hit harder. That is what these softer images do for me, and why they hold up over time.

It’s the same reason we still freeze when looking at a man jumping over a puddle in Paris, or soldiers wading through the surf on Omaha Beach. Those iconic frames are far from sharp. Because they aren't technically perfect, they force the viewer's mind and heart to fill in the gaps and feel the reality of the moment.

A raw, honest, imperfect photograph will beat out a sterile, over-edited digital image every single time. You can engineer technical perfection, but you can’t engineer a feeling.

Long live imperfection.

items.title: Sun, Shadows and Stone: An afternoon at Valle dei Templi
items.summary: As we drive into the parking lot of the Valle dei Templi, there's sand and dust everywhere. It's early August and Ferragosto hasn't started yet, but it feels like the whole of Italy has planned to come here today. Cars crisscross the terrain like ants,…
items.content_html:
As we drive into the parking lot of the Valle dei Templi, there's sand and dust everywhere. It's early August and Ferragosto hasn't started yet, but it feels like the whole of Italy has planned to come here today. Cars crisscross the terrain like ants, and — in typical Sicilian fashion — there's little signage to tell you where to go. After all these years of traveling to Sicily, I've grown used to a bit of organized chaos. I like it, actually. It makes the island feel so much like itself — a stark contrast to the planned, orderly street architecture I'm used to in the Netherlands.

Today I won't have many opportunities to take photos. Still, when the moment arises, I attempt a few shots. I don't want to disturb our guide as he talks — which he does so well — walking us through the complete history of the valley in just over two hours. For the pictures I do manage to shoot, I've set my camera to RAW. It helps preserve the highlights under this burning sun. What I sometimes like to do in these situations is shoot deliberately into the sun. It gives you a silhouetted foreground, and paired with a vintage 50mm Takumar lens, it creates a really beautiful, warm vintage look.

We conclude the day entirely satisfied. This was such a rich experience. It's incredible to witness how these ancient structures have survived destruction, wars, and natural disasters over the millennia, yet they are still standing — a testament to the people who built them. They knew a thing or two about construction, and so much more besides: agriculture, astronomy, mathematics — things we, 2000 years later, can still learn from. This visit definitely deserves a follow-up in the form of a good book about these temples. Or who knows — perhaps I'll visit them again someday. They're not in a hurry, after all.

For now, it's back to the dusty parking lot to queue up with my ant friends. I forget about the ancient Greeks for a moment as my mind slowly drifts to granitas and an ice-cold Peroni.
